The Acts of the Apostles: Growth and expansion of the church; paul the Apostle; other aspects of human experience (part 2)

  2. Mission 2The man hunting Jesus' followers became their greatest missionary. What changed him, and where did he go?

Mission 1

Mission 1: A Jewish fisherman is told in a dream to eat forbidden food. What did it really mean?

Make a guess: A Jewish fisherman is told in a dream to eat forbidden food. What did it really mean?

Mission 1

Peter on the move (9:32–43)

  • After Jerusalem, Peter tours Judea: at Lydda he heals Aeneas; at Joppa he raises Tabitha (Dorcas).
  • "He stayed many days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon." (Acts 9:43, WEBBE) Tanning handled dead animals: an unattractive trade for an observant Jew. Many commentators see a first loosening.
  • So far, Peter's hearers have all been Jews (Acts 2–5) or Samaritans (8:14–25).
  • Caesarea, about 50 km north of Joppa: Rome's administrative capital of Judea, largely Gentile.
Mission 1

Cornelius (10:1–8)

  • "A centurion of what was called the Italian Regiment" (10:1): a Roman officer over about 80 men.
  • "A devout man, and one who feared God with all his house, who gave gifts for the needy generously… and always prayed to God." (Acts 10:2, WEBBE)
  • A God-fearer: a Gentile who worshipped Israel's God and kept some customs, but was not circumcised (not a proselyte).
  • At "about the ninth hour" (3 p.m., a Jewish hour of prayer) an angel tells him to send for Simon Peter at Joppa (10:3–6). His prayers and alms "have gone up for a memorial before God" (10:4).
Mission 1

Peter's vision (10:9–23)

  • At noon, hungry, on the roof, Peter sees a sheet let down holding "all kinds of four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, reptiles, and birds" (10:12).
  • "Rise, Peter, kill and eat!" "Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean." (10:13–14)
  • "What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean." (Acts 10:15, WEBBE) It happens three times (10:16).
  • Background: the kashrut food laws of Leviticus 11 marked Israel as distinct; table fellowship with Gentiles was widely avoided.
  • While he ponders the vision, Cornelius' messengers arrive; the Spirit says go with them, "doubting nothing" (10:19–20). Peter lodges them: Gentiles under his roof.
Mission 1Read the source

No one unclean

> "You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation, but God has shown me that I shouldn't call any man unholy or unclean." (Acts 10:28, WEBBE)

> "Truly I perceive that God doesn't show favouritism; but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him." (Acts 10:34–35, WEBBE)

Q1 How does Peter himself interpret the vision of animals?

Show answer

About people: no person is to be called unclean; not only about food.

Q2 What does "I perceive" in 10:34 show about Peter?

Show answer

He is learning something new: his own view changes during the event.

  • "Unlawful" (10:28) states a common custom of separation; the Torah does not forbid visiting Gentiles outright.
Mission 1

The speech and the "Gentile Pentecost" (10:34–48)

  • Peter's speech follows the kerygma: Jesus anointed "with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good" (10:38); killed; raised on the third day; witnesses who "ate and drank with him" (10:41); judge of living and dead; forgiveness through his name (10:43).
  • "While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the word." (Acts 10:44, WEBBE)
  • They speak in tongues (10:46). The Jewish believers with Peter "were amazed" (10:45).
  • "Can anyone forbid these people from being baptised with water? They have received the Holy Spirit just like us." (10:47)
  • Peter stays with them "some days" (10:48): he eats with Gentiles.

Mission 1

Then and now: Peter's two missions

Jerusalem (Acts 2–5)Caesarea (Acts 10)
HearersJews and proselytesGentile God-fearers
SettingTemple, Solomon's PorchA Roman officer's house
Who moves firstPeter preaches; crowds respondGod prepares both men by visions
Spirit and baptismBaptism, then Spirit (2:38)Spirit, then baptism (10:44–48)
PeterConfident leaderHesitant, then learning ("I perceive")
  • The same message, a new audience: in Acts the initiative is God's, not Peter's.
Mission 1

The report in Jerusalem (11:1–18)

  • "Those who were of the circumcision contended with him, saying, 'You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them!'" (Acts 11:2–3, WEBBE) The issue is table fellowship.
  • Peter retells "in order" (11:4): the vision, the Spirit's command "without discriminating" (11:12), six witnesses, the Spirit falling "even as on us at the beginning" (11:15).
  • He recalls Jesus' word: "John indeed baptised in water, but you will be baptised in the Holy Spirit" (11:16).
  • "Who was I, that I could withstand God?" (Acts 11:17, WEBBE)
  • "They held their peace and glorified God, saying, 'Then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life!'" (Acts 11:18, WEBBE)
  • Luke tells the story three times (10, 11, 15:7–11): his sign that it matters.
Mission 1

Impact on Peter, implications for the mission

  • On Peter: his idea of purity changes; he risks his standing with Jewish believers; he becomes the advocate of Gentile inclusion.
  • Acts 15: at the Jerusalem Council Peter cites it: God "made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith" (15:9). The Council does not require circumcision of Gentiles.
  • Antioch: believers "spoke to the Hellenists" (11:20; many manuscripts read "Greeks"); a mixed church grows; Barnabas and Saul are sent from there (13:1–3).
  • But: Paul reports that at Antioch Peter later "drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision" (Galatians 2:12). The change was real but not easy.
Quick check
?In his report to the Jerusalem church (Acts 11), what is Peter's decisive argument for accepting the Gentiles?
Mission 1

Peter's escape from prison (12:1–19)

  • King Herod (Herod Agrippa I, d. AD 44) "killed James, the brother of John, with the sword" (12:2), and arrests Peter at Passover.
  • "Four squads of four soldiers each" guard him (12:4); "constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him" (12:5).
  • An angel; light; "Stand up quickly!" "His chains fell off his hands." (Acts 12:7, WEBBE) The iron gate opens "by itself" (12:10).
  • "Now I truly know that the Lord has sent out his angel and delivered me" (12:11).
  • At Mary's house (mother of John Mark), Rhoda leaves him at the gate "for joy" (12:14); the others say "It is his angel" (12:15).
  • "Tell these things to James and to the brothers." Then "he departed and went to another place." (12:17) Herod has the guards executed (12:19) and soon dies at Caesarea (12:20–23).
Mission 1

Why the escape matters

  • God protects the mission: a king kills an apostle, yet cannot stop the word. "But the word of God grew and multiplied." (12:24)
  • Passover echo: release from a tyrant at the Passover season, the festival of Israel's deliverance (Exodus 12); also echoes of Jesus' passion (arrest at Passover; a woman's news not believed, as in Luke 24:11).
  • Prayer: the church's prayer frames the rescue (12:5, 12).
  • A handover: Peter leaves the stage; James, the Lord's brother (Galatians 1:19), leads in Jerusalem (15:13); from chapter 13 Acts follows Paul.
  • Not a promise of escape: James dies, Peter is freed. Acts does not explain why.
Mission 1Evaluate

Was Cornelius the turning point?

  • Claim: The conversion of Cornelius, not Paul's journeys, was the real turning point of the Gentile mission.
  • For: Luke tells it three times; it is the precedent at the Jerusalem Council (15:7–11).
  • For: it comes through Peter, the leading apostle, so the Jerusalem church cannot dismiss it (11:18).
  • Against: Philip had already baptised an Ethiopian (8:38), and unnamed believers preach to non-Jews at Antioch (11:20).
  • Against: the decisive growth, and the theology of Gentile inclusion (Galatians), come through Paul; Peter himself wavers (Galatians 2:12).
  • Historical questions: some scholars think Luke has shaped a smaller event into a programme; others note that Peter's openness fits Paul's own reports (Galatians 2:7–9).
  • Judgement criteria: a turning point in principle or in numbers? Who decides what Acts treats as a turning point: Luke or history?

Mission 2

Mission 2: The man hunting Jesus' followers became their greatest missionary. What changed him, and where did he go?

Make a guess: The man hunting Jesus' followers became their greatest missionary. What changed him, and where did he go?

Mission 2

Saul before Damascus

  • "Born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel" (Acts 22:3, WEBBE): a diaspora Jew trained in Jerusalem; a Roman citizen (22:28).
  • In his own words: "of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; concerning the law, a Pharisee" (Philippians 3:5, WEBBE).
  • He approved Stephen's death (8:1) and "ravaged the assembly", dragging men and women to prison (8:3).
  • "Still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord", he asks the high priest for letters to arrest followers of "the Way" in Damascus (Acts 9:1–2, WEBBE).
  • Why? Probably zeal for the Law and the one God (Philippians 3:6; Galatians 1:14): a crucified "Messiah" looked like a scandal (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13).
Mission 2

The Damascus road (9:1–9)

  • Near Damascus, "a light from the sky shone around him" (9:3).
  • "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" "Who are you, Lord?" "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting." (Acts 9:4–5, WEBBE)
  • "Me": Jesus identifies himself with his followers. To persecute the church is to persecute him.
  • His companions "stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one" (9:7).
  • Blind for three days, he neither eats nor drinks (9:9): some readers see a death-and-rising pattern.
Mission 2

Ananias and the commission (9:10–19)

  • Ananias, a disciple in Damascus, is told in a vision to go to Saul at the house of Judah on the street called Straight (9:11). He objects: this man is dangerous (9:13–14).
  • The Lord's answer sets out Saul's whole future.
  • Ananias lays hands on him and calls him "Brother Saul" (9:17).
  • "Something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptised." (Acts 9:18, WEBBE)
  • At once "in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God" (9:20). Plots follow; he escapes over the wall in a basket (9:23–25).
  • In Jerusalem the disciples fear him; Barnabas vouches for him (9:26–27).
Mission 2Read the source

Chosen vessel

> "Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name's sake." (Acts 9:15–16, WEBBE)

> "But when it was the good pleasure of God, who separated me from my mother's womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him amongst the Gentiles…" (Galatians 1:15–16, WEBBE)

Q1 Which three audiences are named in Acts 9:15?

Show answer

The nations (Gentiles), kings, and the people of Israel.

Q2 What word in Galatians 1:15 suggests Paul saw the event as a prophet's call?

Show answer

"Called", and "from my mother's womb", echoing Jeremiah 1:5 and Isaiah 49:1.

Mission 2Diversity

Conversion or call?

  • Three accounts in Acts (9; 22:6–16; 26:12–18) differ in detail: the companions hear the sound (9:7) but "didn't understand the voice" (22:9); in ch. 26 the commission comes from Jesus directly, with "It is hard for you to kick against the goads" (26:14).
  • Paul's letters mention it briefly: "he appeared to me also" (1 Corinthians 15:8); a revelation (Galatians 1:12, 16).
  • Conversion: a turn from persecutor to believer; the traditional reading and Acts' focus.
  • Call: Krister Stendahl (1921–2008), Paul Among Jews and Gentiles (1976): Paul did not change religion; he worshipped the same God and was called to a new task, the Gentiles.
  • Naturalistic readings (a seizure, guilt over Stephen, a vision) remain speculative; the texts give little medical evidence.
  • Significance: Paul's apostleship rests on having seen the risen Lord (1 Corinthians 9:1); Christians cite it as the clearest case of grace changing an enemy.
Quick check
?What is the main significance of the words "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting" (Acts 9:5)?
Mission 2

First journey (13:1–14:28)

  • Antioch in Syria: "Separate Barnabas and Saul for me" (13:2). Sent with fasting, prayer and laying on of hands.
  • Cyprus: at Paphos the magician Elymas is blinded; the proconsul Sergius Paulus believes. "Saul, who is also called Paul" (13:9) now leads.
  • Perga: John Mark goes home (13:13).
  • Pisidian Antioch: synagogue sermon; "we turn to the Gentiles" (13:46) (see Mission 3).
  • Iconium, then Lystra: a lame man healed; the crowd calls Barnabas "Jupiter" and Paul "Mercury" (14:12); later Paul is stoned and left for dead (14:19). Derbe.
  • Return: "appointed elders for them in every assembly" (14:23). At Antioch they report that God "had opened a door of faith to the nations" (14:27).
Mission 2

Second journey (15:36–18:22)

  • After the Jerusalem Council (15:1–35) frees Gentiles from circumcision, Paul and Barnabas split over Mark (15:39). Paul takes Silas; Timothy joins at Lystra.
  • "Forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia" (16:6). At Troas: "Come over into Macedonia and help us." (16:9) The first "we" passage (16:10): Europe.
  • Philippi: Lydia baptised; a slave girl freed from a spirit; Paul and Silas beaten and jailed; earthquake; Paul and Silas tell the jailer: "Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved" (16:31).
  • Thessalonica: "These who have turned the world upside down have come here also" (17:6). Berea: hearers examine the Scriptures daily (17:11). Athens (see Mission 3).
  • Corinth: tentmaking with Aquila and Priscilla (18:3); 18 months (18:11); the proconsul Gallio refuses to try Paul (18:12–17). Back via Ephesus to Caesarea and Antioch (18:22).
Mission 2

Third journey (18:23–21:17)

  • Through Galatia and Phrygia, "establishing all the disciples" (18:23).
  • Ephesus, about three years (20:31): twelve disciples of John receive the Spirit (19:1–7); daily teaching in the school of Tyrannus, "so that all those who lived in Asia heard the word" (19:10).
  • Riot: the silversmith Demetrius fears for the trade in shrines; "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" (19:28).
  • Macedonia and Greece; at Troas Eutychus falls from a window and is restored (20:9–12).
  • Miletus: farewell to the Ephesian elders: "It is more blessed to give than to receive" (20:35).
  • To Jerusalem despite warnings (Agabus, 21:10–11): "I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem" (21:13).
Quick check
?On which missionary journey did Paul first take the Gospel into Europe?
Mission 2

Paul's method

  • Synagogue first (13:5, 14; 17:2): Jews and God-fearers, then Gentiles. "It was necessary that God's word should be spoken to you first." (13:46)
  • Cities on trade routes: Roman roads, sea lanes, a shared language (koine Greek), Roman peace.
  • Self-support: tentmaking (18:3; 20:34), so the message is free.
  • Teams: Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, the "we" narrator (traditionally Luke), Priscilla and Aquila.
  • Adaptation: scripture in the synagogue, creation and conscience with pagans (14:15–17; 17:22–31). "I have become all things to all men" (1 Corinthians 9:22).
  • Follow-up: return visits, appointed elders, and letters (Galatians, 1 Corinthians, Ephesians: A2 unit).
Mission 2

Significance of the journeys

  • A Jewish messianic movement becomes a multi-ethnic one across the Roman east: Acts 1:8 "to the uttermost parts of the earth".
  • Opposition and suffering shape the mission (14:22; 2 Corinthians 11:23–27): mobs, courts, prison.
  • Roman officials (Sergius Paulus, Gallio, the Ephesian town clerk) mostly find no crime: often read as part of Luke's case that the faith is no threat to Rome.
  • Churches founded in Galatia, Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth and Ephesus later receive Paul's letters: the earliest surviving Christian writings.
  • Pattern for later mission: city centres, local leaders, translation of the message into new cultures.
Mission 2Evaluate

Is mission essential to the spread of belief?

  • Claim: Deliberate mission is the most important factor in the spread of religious belief.
  • For: Acts and Paul's churches; the commands of Matthew 28:19 and Acts 1:8; later movements (monastic missions to Ireland and Britain; modern growth in Africa, Asia and Latin America).
  • For: many religions spread by invitation and teaching: Buddhist missionaries under Ashoka; Islamic da'wah.
  • Against: much growth comes from family, birth rates, migration and trade, not missionaries.
  • Against: mission linked with empire and colonialism damaged trust; some argue for dialogue and witness by example rather than conversion. Most Jewish communities, for example, accept converts but do not seek them.
  • Today: pluralist and secular contexts; online evangelism; inter-faith respect.
  • Judgement criteria: Spread in numbers or depth? Mission as preaching, service or both? Is it fair to judge Paul's mission by later abuses?

Mission 3

Mission 3: Paul preached in a synagogue and to Greek philosophers. Did he change his message, or only his words?

Make a guess: Paul preached in a synagogue and to Greek philosophers. Did he change his message, or only his words?

Mission 3

Two speeches, two worlds

  • Acts gives one full sample of Paul preaching to Jews and God-fearers (Pisidian Antioch, Acts 13) and one to pagan Greeks (Athens, Acts 17).
  • A third, short one at Lystra (14:15–17) is a sketch of the pagan version.
  • Ancient historians composed speeches to fit speaker and setting; how close these are to Paul's words is debated.
  • Read both for: content (what is said), theology (what it claims about God and Jesus), cultural significance (how it fits the hearers).
Mission 3

A sermon in the synagogue (13:13–16)

  • Antioch of Pisidia: a Roman colony in the uplands of Asia Minor; a Jewish community with a synagogue; Gentile God-fearers attend.
  • Sabbath service: "After the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers of the synagogue" invite any "word of exhortation for the people" (13:15).
  • Paul stands: "Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen." (Acts 13:16, WEBBE) Two audiences named at once.
  • The form is close to a synagogue homily: history, scripture texts, application.
Mission 3

Content at Pisidian Antioch (13:17–41)

  • Israel's story (13:17–22): God "chose our fathers", the Exodus "with an uplifted arm", judges, Saul, then David, "a man after my heart".
  • From David to Jesus (13:23–25): "From this man's offspring, God has brought salvation to Israel"; John the Baptist prepares.
  • Death (13:26–29): Jerusalem's people and rulers did not recognise him and so "fulfilled" the prophets by condemning him.
  • Resurrection (13:30–37): "But God raised him from the dead"; proofs from Psalm 2:7 ("You are my Son"), Isaiah 55:3 ("the holy and sure blessings of David") and Psalm 16:10 ("You will not allow your Holy One to see decay"). David decayed; Jesus did not.
  • Offer and warning (13:38–41): forgiveness and justification; Habakkuk 1:5, "Behold, you scoffers!"
  • Close to Peter's speeches, plus one Pauline note.
Mission 3Read the source

Justified by him

> "Be it known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man is proclaimed to you remission of sins; and by him everyone who believes is justified from all things, from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses." (Acts 13:38–39, WEBBE)

Q1 What two gifts are offered "through this man"?

Show answer

Remission (forgiveness) of sins and justification.

Q2 Which phrase anticipates the theme of Galatians?

Show answer

"Justified from all things, from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses": in Paul's teaching, believing in Jesus, not keeping the Law, puts people right with God.

Quick check
?Why does Paul quote Psalm 16:10 ("You will not allow your Holy One to see decay") at Pisidian Antioch?
Mission 3

The turn to the Gentiles (13:42–52)

  • Many Jews and "devout proselytes" follow Paul and Barnabas (13:43). "The next Sabbath, almost the whole city was gathered together" (13:44).
  • Seeing the crowds, some of the Jewish hearers, "filled with jealousy", contradict Paul (13:45).
  • "It was necessary that God's word should be spoken to you first… behold, we turn to the Gentiles." (Acts 13:46, WEBBE)
  • Isaiah 49:6: "I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth." (Acts 13:47, WEBBE)
  • Gentiles rejoice; opponents stir "devout and prominent women" and leading men; Paul and Barnabas shake the dust off their feet (13:50–51) but leave a church "filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit" (13:52).
  • The turn is local: in the next city Paul goes to the synagogue again (14:1).
Mission 3

Athens: the setting (17:16–21)

  • Paul's "spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols" (17:16).
  • He reasons in the synagogue and "in the marketplace" (the Agora) daily (17:17), like Socrates.
  • Epicureans: gods remote and unconcerned; the goal is tranquillity; no life after death. Stoics: a divine reason (logos) pervades the world; live by nature and virtue.
  • "What does this babbler want to say?" (spermologos, seed-picker); "foreign deities", "because he preached Jesus and the resurrection" (17:18): perhaps heard as two gods, Jesus and Anastasis.
  • Taken to the Areopagus (the hill of Ares, and the council that met there): a hearing on new teaching, possibly formal.
Mission 3

Content at Athens (17:22–31)

  • Point of contact: "very religious"; an altar "TO AN UNKNOWN GOD": "What therefore you worship in ignorance, I announce to you." (17:22–23)
  • God the creator: makes all things; "doesn't dwell in temples made with hands" (17:24); needs nothing; gives "life and breath" (17:25).
  • One humanity: "from one blood every nation" (17:26), made to seek God, "though he is not far from each one of us" (17:27).
  • Greek poets: "For in him we live, move, and have our being"; "For we are also his offspring" (17:28). So God is not "like gold, or silver, or stone" (17:29).
  • Turn: "The times of ignorance therefore God overlooked. But now he commands that all people everywhere should repent" (17:30).
  • Judgement by "the man whom he has ordained", assured by raising him from the dead (17:31). Jesus is not named.
Mission 3Read the source

Your own poets

> "The God who made the world and all things in it, he, being Lord of heaven and earth, doesn't dwell in temples made with hands." (Acts 17:24, WEBBE)

> "'For in him we live, move, and have our being.' As some of your own poets have said, 'For we are also his offspring.'" (Acts 17:28, WEBBE)

  • "His offspring" is from Aratus (3rd century BC), Phaenomena line 5, a Stoic poet from Cilicia. The first line is often attributed to Epimenides of Crete (uncertain).

Q1 Which Jewish belief does 17:24 share with Stephen's speech?

Show answer

God does not live in temples made with hands: 7:48.

Q2 Why quote pagan poets rather than the Psalms?

Show answer

The hearers do not accept Jewish scripture; Paul starts from what they already grant.

Mission 3

The reaction (17:32–34)

  • "When they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others said, 'We want to hear you again concerning this.'" (Acts 17:32, WEBBE)
  • Greek thought widely valued the soul's release from the body; a bodily resurrection seemed absurd.
  • A few believe: "Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others" (17:34): a council member and a woman named in a scene of men.
  • No church at Athens is mentioned again in Acts; Paul moves on to Corinth (18:1).
Mission 3Diversity

Two speeches compared

Pisidian AntiochAthens
HearersJews, proselytes, God-fearersPhilosophers, curious Athenians
Starting pointIsrael's historyAn altar; creation; human search
AuthorityTorah, Prophets, PsalmsReason, Greek poets
JesusNamed; Son of David, raised, forgives, justifiesUnnamed "man"; judge, raised
CallBelieve; warning to scoffersRepent; judgement coming
OutcomeLarge response; then oppositionMockery; a few believe
  • Constant: one God, the resurrection, a call to respond. Variable: language, evidence, starting point.
Quick check
?What is the main way the Athens speech is adapted to its audience?
Mission 3Evaluate

Was Athens a wise adaptation or a failure?

  • Claim: The Areopagus speech compromised the Christian message and failed.
  • Failure: few converts; no church. W. M. Ramsay (1851–1939), St Paul the Traveller and the Roman Citizen (1895), thought Paul, disappointed, resolved at Corinth to preach only the cross (paraphrase): "I determined not to know anything amongst you except Jesus Christ and him crucified." (1 Corinthians 2:2, WEBBE)
  • Not Paul's speech: Martin Dibelius (1883–1947), "Paul on the Areopagus" (1939), saw a Hellenistic, Stoic-coloured sermon foreign to the letters; Philipp Vielhauer (1914–1977) argued its natural theology differs from Romans 1 (paraphrase).
  • Defence: F. F. Bruce (1910–1990) and others: the core is biblical (creation, idolatry, judgement, resurrection), like Romans 1:20 and Lystra (14:15–17); the speech is a start, not a whole course.
  • Success: Dionysius and Damaris believe; the model of starting from the hearers' culture is still used in mission and inter-faith dialogue.
  • Judgement criteria: success measured by numbers or faithfulness? Does using another culture's ideas inevitably change the message? How Pauline is Luke's Paul?
Mission check

?A Christian chaplain at a secular university wants to speak to students with no religious background. Following the Athens speech rather than Pisidian Antioch, which approach would she take?

Mission 4: How did a small prayer meeting in Los Angeles become a quarter of world Christianity?

Make a guess: How did a small prayer meeting in Los Angeles become a quarter of world Christianity?

Mission 4

Roots: Topeka and Azusa Street

  • 1901, Topeka, Kansas: at Charles Parham's Bible school, Agnes Ozman speaks in tongues. Parham teaches tongues as the "initial evidence" of baptism in the Spirit.
  • 1906–c. 1909, Azusa Street, Los Angeles: William J. Seymour (1870–1922), an African American preacher, leads a revival in a former stable building. Meetings for hours each day, Black and white, rich and poor, women and men together: unusual in segregated America.
  • Missionaries and a newspaper, The Apostolic Faith, spread it to Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America within a few years.
  • Pentecostal denominations form: Church of God in Christ (Pentecostal from 1907), Assemblies of God (USA, 1914), Elim (UK, 1915).
  • Roots also in the Holiness movement and earlier revivals (e.g. Wales, 1904–05).
Mission 4Read the source

The Spirit at Pentecost

> "Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak." (Acts 2:3–4, WEBBE)

> "But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all." (1 Corinthians 12:7, WEBBE)

  • Paul then lists gifts: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, languages (tongues) and their interpretation (1 Corinthians 12:8–10).

Q1 Why do Pentecostals take their name from Acts 2?

Show answer

They expect the same filling with the Spirit, with tongues, today.

Q2 According to 1 Corinthians 12:7, who are the gifts for?

Show answer

For the good of the whole community, not for private status.

Mission 4

Main beliefs

  • Baptism in the Holy Spirit: a powerful experience of being filled with the Spirit. Classical Pentecostals: a second experience after conversion, usually shown by speaking in tongues (glossolalia).
  • Gifts of the Spirit (charismata, hence "charismatic") are for today: tongues, prophecy, healing, words of knowledge.
  • The "Fourfold Gospel": Jesus as Saviour, Baptiser in the Spirit, Healer and Coming King.
  • The Bible as the authority; personal conversion; evangelism.
  • Worship: lively, participatory, expectant: raised hands, spontaneous prayer, testimony, healing prayer.
  • Not all Pentecostals agree that tongues are the necessary evidence; many charismatics do not.
Mission 4

The Charismatic Movement after 1960

  • Charismatic = Pentecostal-style experience inside the historic churches, without leaving them.
  • 1960: Dennis Bennett, an Episcopal priest in Van Nuys, California, tells his congregation he has spoken in tongues; the news spreads nationally.
  • 1964 (UK): Anglican Michael Harper founds the Fountain Trust to support renewal across denominations.
  • 1967: the Duquesne Weekend (Pittsburgh) begins the Catholic Charismatic Renewal.
  • 1980s–90s: John Wimber's Vineyard churches ("signs and wonders"); the "Toronto Blessing" (1994); the Alpha course (Holy Trinity Brompton, London) with its Holy Spirit weekend.
  • Charismatics in sacramental churches often see Spirit baptism as a release of grace already given in baptism and confirmation, not a second blessing.
Quick check
?What best distinguishes the Charismatic Movement from classical Pentecostalism?
Mission 4

Global growth

  • Evangelicalism: defined by historian David Bebbington (Evangelicalism in Modern Britain, 1989) by four marks: Bible authority, the cross, conversion, activism. Global networks such as the Lausanne Movement (1974).
  • Pentecostal and Charismatic Christians: about 584 million in 2010, over a quarter of all Christians (Pew Research Center, 2011).
  • US: Assemblies of God and Church of God in Christ; televangelism and megachurches; strong growth among Hispanic Americans.
  • Beyond: Latin America (e.g. Brazil's Assemblies of God), Africa (e.g. Nigeria, Ghana), Asia (e.g. Yoido Full Gospel Church, Seoul). Most Pentecostals now live in the Global South.
  • Why it spreads: direct experience, healing, lay leadership, local languages and music, help for people moving to cities.
Mission 4

Impact on believers and communities

  • Believers: a sense of God's closeness, assurance, healing, freedom from addiction; a new moral discipline.
  • Lay empowerment: anyone can receive gifts and minister; in many churches women preach and lead (e.g. Aimee Semple McPherson, 1920s), though others restrict leadership.
  • Communities: support for migrants (jobs, housing, language, belonging); growth where other churches decline; renewal in historic churches (e.g. Alpha).
  • Tensions: congregations split over tongues in the 1960s–70s; authoritarian leaders in some churches.
  • Prosperity gospel: some teach that faith brings health and wealth; many Pentecostals and other Christians criticise this as unbiblical.
  • Cessationists (e.g. B. B. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles, 1918) argue that miraculous gifts ended with the apostles (cf. 1 Corinthians 13:8).
Quick check
?Which factor has most helped Pentecostal churches spread among migrants in European cities?
Mission 4

Challenge 1: can the experience be verified?

  • Verification: a claim is meaningful or justified only if it can be checked by experience others can test (logical positivism: A. J. Ayer, 1910–1989, Language, Truth and Logic, 1936).
  • A person who says "the Holy Spirit filled me" reports a private experience. How could anyone else, or even the person, check that the cause is God?
  • Counterfeits: Paul himself requires "discerning of spirits" (1 Corinthians 12:10) and order in worship (1 Corinthians 14:27, 40).
  • Response: Richard Swinburne (b. 1934), The Existence of God (1979): the principle of credulity: trust how things seem unless there is a special reason not to; and the principle of testimony: believe others' reports unless there is reason to doubt them.
  • Reply: experiences of God are unlike sense experience: there are no agreed checks, so credulity may not apply.
Mission 4

Challenge 2: natural explanation

  • Linguistics: William Samarin, Tongues of Men and Angels (1972): glossolalia sounds like language but lacks consistent grammar and meaning; it can be learned.
  • Psychology: expectation, group suggestion and music can produce falling, laughter or ecstatic speech (critics' reading of the "Toronto Blessing").
  • Neuroscience: brain scans during tongues show changed activity (e.g. reduced activity in frontal lobes: Newberg et al., 2006).
  • Response 1: a natural mechanism does not rule out a divine cause; God may work through brain and body (compare contingency miracles).
  • Response 2: judge by fruits. William James: "By their fruits ye shall know them, not by their roots" (The Varieties of Religious Experience, 1902, Lecture I).
  • Response 3: many Pentecostals accept that tongues are often not a known human language; Paul says the speaker "speaks not to men, but to God" (1 Corinthians 14:2, WEBBE).
Mission 4Evaluate

Does a natural explanation take away the religious value?

  • Claim: If charismatic experiences have a natural explanation, they have no religious value.
  • For: if the same effects come from suggestion or learning, God is not needed to explain them (Occam's razor).
  • For: unverifiable claims (ones no one else can check) cannot ground authority, especially when leaders use them to control others.
  • Against: natural process and divine action need not compete; value may lie in transformed lives (James' fruits).
  • Against: Richard Swinburne's principle of credulity (trust how things seem unless there is a special reason not to): millions report such experiences; the burden is on the sceptic.
  • Strengths and weaknesses of the movement: renewal, growth, lay participation, care for migrants vs division, emotionalism, prosperity teaching.
  • Judgement criteria: Does explaining how answer whether God is involved? What counts as evidence of the Spirit? How should fruits be measured?
Quick check
?A researcher shows that people who speak in tongues can learn the skill and that it lacks the grammar of a human language. Which reply would a Pentecostal most likely make?
Mission check

?A Catholic parish in Ireland starts a weekly prayer group where people pray for healing and some speak in tongues. The parish still celebrates Mass, and the members stay Catholic. How is this group best described?

The same experiences of the Spirit can lead people out into new churches (Pentecostal) or renew the churches they already belong to (Charismatic).

Mission 5

Mission 5: Missionaries once sailed from Britain to the world. Why do some now come to Britain to do the same?

Make a guess: Missionaries once sailed from Britain to the world. Why do some now come to Britain to do the same?

Mission 5

What Christians mean by mission

  • Mission (Latin mittere, to send): the Church's task of being sent into the world.
  • Evangelism: one part of mission: sharing the gospel ("good news") of Jesus so that people may come to faith.
  • Many Christians also count service (care, healing, education), justice and dialogue as mission.
  • Debates in this mission: Is mission mainly about converting people? Who sends whom? How should Christians share faith among people of other religions and none?
Mission 5Read the source

The Great Commission

> "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you." (Matthew 28:19–20, WEBBE)

> "You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth." (Acts 1:8, WEBBE)

  • Christians take these words of the risen Jesus as the mandate for mission.

Q1 Which three activities does Matthew 28:19–20 name?

Show answer

Making disciples, baptising, teaching.

Q2 Why might Acts 1:8 suggest that mission spreads outward from a centre?

Show answer

It moves from Jerusalem, to the surrounding regions, to the ends of the earth.

Mission 5

Edinburgh 1910

  • World Missionary Conference, Edinburgh, June 1910: about 1,200 delegates, almost all from Protestant missionary societies of Europe and North America.
  • Chair: John R. Mott (1865–1955), American Methodist layman. Mood: confident. The watchword of the Student Volunteer Movement was "the evangelization of the world in this generation".
  • Mission was pictured as going from the "Christian West" to the "non-Christian world".
  • Only a handful of delegates came from Asia. V. S. Azariah (1874–1945), later the first Indian Anglican bishop, pleaded with Western missionaries: "Give us FRIENDS!"
  • Legacy: cooperation instead of competition between missions; it led to the International Missionary Council (1921) and the ecumenical movement.
Mission 5

Missionary outreach, 1800–1960

  • Protestant societies: Baptist Missionary Society (1792; William Carey in India), London Missionary Society (1795), Church Missionary Society (1799), China Inland Mission (1865; Hudson Taylor).
  • Methods: preaching; Bible translation into local languages; schools and hospitals; training local leaders. Henry Venn (CMS) aimed at "three-self" churches: self-governing, self-supporting, self-propagating.
  • Catholic orders: Jesuits, Spiritans (Holy Ghost Fathers), Columbans, women's congregations running schools and clinics.
  • Irish outreach: the Presbyterian Church in Ireland sent its first missionaries to Gujarat, India (1841) and later to Manchuria; Amy Carmichael (1867–1951) from Millisle, Co. Down, founded the Dohnavur Fellowship in south India; the Maynooth Mission to China (1916, the Columbans); Bishop Joseph Shanahan in Nigeria; Mother Mary Martin founded the Medical Missionaries of Mary (1937).
  • Impact, debated: education, medicine and literacy spread, and churches grew; but mission was often tied to colonial power and Western culture. Many African and Asian churches grew fastest through local evangelists, often after missionaries left.
Mission 5

How ideas of mission changed

  • 1910, Edinburgh: mission pictured as going from the "Christian West" to the "non-Christian world".
  • 1952, Willingen: mission is missio Dei, God's own mission; the Church does not own mission but takes part in what God is already doing.
  • 1963, Mexico City: "mission in six continents": every continent, the West included, is a mission field.
  • 1965, Vatican II, Ad Gentes: the whole Church is missionary by its nature. 1975, Evangelii Nuntiandi (Paul VI): evangelisation includes witness of life and changing society.
  • 1974, Lausanne Congress (evangelicals; John Stott, Billy Graham): evangelism and social action are both Christian duty.
  • 1984–90, Anglican Five Marks of Mission: tell, teach, tend, transform, treasure creation.
  • Shift in short: from sending to "heathen lands" to mission from everywhere to everywhere, with word and deed.
Mission 5Diversity

Different emphases today

  • Evangelical (Lausanne Covenant, 1974): social action matters, but "evangelism is primary" (para. 6). Conversion to Christ is the heart of mission.
  • Catholic: evangelisation is the Church's deepest identity; John Paul II's new evangelisation (from 1983) for once-Christian societies; Francis, Evangelii Gaudium (2013): every baptised person is a "missionary disciple".
  • Ecumenical / liberal Protestant (WCC): mission as presence, justice and reconciliation; some are wary of seeking converts.
  • Orthodox: mission flows from worship: "the liturgy after the liturgy", Christians living out the Eucharist in the world.
  • Pentecostal: mission as Spirit-empowered witness, expecting healing and signs (Acts 1:8); often described as the fastest-growing form worldwide.
Quick check
?Which development changed Christian thinking by treating mission as God's own activity, in which the Church takes part?
Mission 5

Reverse mission

  • By the late 20th century most Christians lived in the global South (Africa, Asia, Latin America). Andrew Walls (1928–2021) and Philip Jenkins (The Next Christendom, 2002) traced this shift.
  • Reverse mission: Christians from former mission fields come to evangelise Europe and Britain, which they see as having drifted from faith.
  • Examples: the Redeemed Christian Church of God (founded in Nigeria, 1952; UK parishes since the late 1980s); Kingsway International Christian Centre (London, 1992); Latin American and Korean churches; Polish Catholic priests serving migrants.
  • Forerunner: Lesslie Newbigin (1909–1998), back from nearly forty years in India, argued that Western culture itself is a mission field (Foolishness to the Greeks, 1986).
  • Debate: research suggests many such churches mostly reach people of their own diaspora; leaders and scholars disagree about how far they reach white British people.
Mission 5

Evangelism in a pluralist, secular age

  • Pluralism: many faiths side by side; claims that one faith is uniquely true can seem arrogant. Secularisation: religion has less public weight.
  • Newbigin: in a pluralist society Christians should offer the gospel as public truth, humbly, not as private opinion.
  • Methods: courses such as Alpha (from Holy Trinity Brompton, London; widely used since the 1990s); Fresh Expressions of church; social action (foodbanks, street pastors); online and social media witness.
  • Objections: evangelism may disrespect other faiths or exploit vulnerable people; secular critics, and some Christians, prefer presence and service.
  • Replies: freedom of religion includes freedom to share and change belief; Christians are told to give a reason for their hope "with humility and fear" (1 Peter 3:15).
  • Your spec frames this as outreach "in the context of secularisation and modern atheistic thinking".
Quick check
?Which description best fits the reverse mission movement?
Mission 5Evaluate

Is mission still relevant to the spread of Christianity?

  • Claim: Mission and evangelism are no longer appropriate in a pluralist, secular society.
  • For: Many people see seeking converts as disrespectful of other faiths and of non-belief.
  • For: The link between historic mission and colonialism damaged trust.
  • Against: Christianity grew worldwide in the 20th century largely through local evangelism; mission still spreads belief.
  • Against: Mission has broadened: service, justice and dialogue sit beside proclamation (e.g. the Five Marks of Mission).
  • Against: Reverse mission shows that former mission fields still see evangelism as good news to share.
  • Judgement criteria: What counts as mission (conversion only, or word and deed)? Is respect compatible with seeking to persuade? Is the UK a mission field?
Mission check

?A church in Leeds is led by a pastor from Ghana. It runs a foodbank, holds a weekly course explaining the Christian faith, and joins an iftar meal at a local mosque. A critic says: "That isn't mission. Mission means sending people overseas to convert others." Which reply best reflects how Christian ideas of mission have developed since 1910?

The direction of mission has turned around, and its meaning has widened. Next: how mission at Edinburgh 1910 also started the search for Christian unity.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Cornelius, a God-fearing centurion, and Peter are both prepared by visions; Peter learns "I shouldn't call any man unholy or unclean" (10:28), and the Spirit falls on Gentiles before baptism.
  • In Jerusalem Peter defends eating with Gentiles: "who was I, that I could withstand God?" (11:17); the church accepts Gentile repentance, a precedent for Acts 15.
  • Peter's escape from Herod (12:1–19) shows God protecting the word; Peter leaves, James leads in Jerusalem, and Acts turns to Paul.

Mission 2

  • Saul the persecutor meets the risen Jesus on the Damascus road ("why do you persecute me?"), is healed and baptised through Ananias and commissioned as a "chosen vessel" (9:15); read as conversion or as a prophetic call (Stendahl).
  • Journey 1: Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, Lystra; "a door of faith to the nations". Journey 2: Council aftermath, Macedonia, Philippi, Athens, Corinth. Journey 3: Ephesus, riot, Miletus farewell, Jerusalem.
  • Method: synagogue first, cities, self-support, teams, adaptation, letters. Mission's role in spreading belief today is debated.

Mission 3

  • Pisidian Antioch (13:16–41): Israel's history, Davidic promise, death, resurrection proved from Psalms 2 and 16 and Isaiah 55, forgiveness and justification "not by the law of Moses"; the turn to the Gentiles (13:46–47).
  • Athens (17:22–31): unknown god, creator not in temples, one humanity, Greek poets (Aratus), repentance, judgement by a man raised from the dead; mockery and a few believers.
  • Same core, different starting point; scholars debate whether Athens was a failure (Ramsay), un-Pauline (Dibelius, Vielhauer) or a sound model (Bruce).

Mission 4

  • Pentecostalism: Topeka (1901) and Azusa Street (1906, Seymour); Spirit baptism, tongues, healing, the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12.
  • Charismatic Movement (from 1960): renewal within historic churches (Bennett, Fountain Trust, Catholic Renewal 1967).
  • Challenges: verification and natural explanation; responses: credulity and testimony (Swinburne), mechanism is not cause, fruits (James).

Mission 5

  • Mission is the Church being sent (Matthew 28:19–20); evangelism is one part of it.
  • Since 1910 the picture changed: from West-to-rest conversion to missio Dei and mission from everywhere to everywhere, in word and deed; reverse mission sends Christians from the global South to Britain.
  • 19th–20th-century outreach, including Irish missions, spread schools, hospitals and churches, but was tangled with colonialism.
